overview:
Gommatasara, composed by Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti (c. 10th–11th century CE), is one of the most systematic Digambara Jain treatises on the nature of the soul (jiva) and karmic bondage. The work is divided broadly into two major sections: Jiva-kanda (the soul) and Karma-kanda (karmic matter). The Karma-kanda, especially, is a technical exposition of the ontology, classification, operation, and cessation of karma, and it stands as a cornerstone for later Digambara doctrinal elaborations on karmic theory.

In Gommatasara’s Karma-kanda, karma is treated as a subtle form of pudgala (matter) that binds to the soul due to the soul’s own activities (yoga) under the influence of passions (kasaya). Nemichandra begins by affirming the eternal relationship between jiva and karmic matter, describing this union as the soul’s “prakriti,” “shila,” or “svabhava”—its nature. Karma is not merely metaphorical; it is a real, material entity that obscures the innate qualities of the soul such as infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. The text emphasizes that the bondage of karma is beginningless, yet it is not endless: through right faith (samyaktva), right knowledge (samyag-jnana), and right conduct (samyag-charitra), the inflow (asrava) of new karmas can be stopped (samvara) and existing karmas can be shed (nirjara), culminating in liberation (moksha).

Gommatasara offers a highly detailed taxonomy of karmas. It distinguishes the eight primary types (prakriti) of karma: knowledge-obscuring (jnanavaraniya), perception-obscuring (darsanavaraniya), feeling-producing (vedaniya), deluding (mohaniya), obstructive (antaraya), age-determining (ayushya), body-making (namakarma), and status-determining (gotra). Within these, Nemichandra enumerates numerous subtypes—148 karmic sub-classes in total—each with specific functions and modes of operation. The text explains how these karmas differ in terms of intensity, duration, quantity, and space-points of bondage, and how they correspond to the fourteen spiritual stages (gunasthanas) through which the soul progresses.

A central feature of Gommatasara’s treatment of karma is its integration with the doctrine of gunasthanas. The fourteen stages—from mithyatva (wrong belief) to ayoga-kevali (the stage just before liberation)—are mapped against the presence, subsidence, destruction, or mixed states (ksaya, upashama, ksayopashama) of various karmas, especially the deluding (mohaniya) karma. Nemichandra shows how specific karmic configurations give rise to particular spiritual conditions, and how the gradual purification of the soul is essentially a process of transforming its karmic profile. This tight linkage between karmic states and spiritual stages makes Gommatasara a technical manual for understanding the soul’s journey.

The Karma-kanda also discusses the mechanisms of karmic inflow and bondage. Inflow (asrava) occurs through the activities of body, speech, and mind (yoga), when these are accompanied by passions such as anger, pride, deceit, and greed. Bondage (bandha) is classified according to four parameters: type (prakriti), duration (sthiti), intensity (anubhaga), and quantity (pradesha). Nemichandra explains how different ethical and spiritual practices influence each of these parameters—for instance, how vows, austerities, and meditation can reduce the duration and intensity of karmas, and how severe passions increase them. This analytical framework allows practitioners and scholars to conceptualize spiritual progress in precise karmic terms.

Another important contribution of Gommatasara is its explanation of non-destructive versus destructive karmas. The first four—knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, and deluding—are classified as ghatiya (destructive) karmas because they directly impair the essential qualities of the soul. The remaining four—obstructive, age, body-making, and status—are aghatiya (non-destructive) karmas, affecting the external conditions of existence rather than the intrinsic nature of the soul. Nemichandra’s ordering of these karmas is deliberate and doctrinally significant: for example, he places feeling-producing karma among the destructive karmas and explains its relation to deluding karma, showing how pleasure and pain experiences are intertwined with delusion.

Throughout the Karma-kanda, Nemichandra draws on earlier canonical and post-canonical Jain sources, but he systematizes them in a way that is numerically and logically rigorous. The text uses extensive numerical classifications, combinatorial schemes, and technical terminology to describe karmic states, making it a key resource for advanced study of Jain karma theory. At the same time, Gommatasara maintains a soteriological focus: the ultimate aim of understanding karma is not mere intellectual mastery but the practical realization of liberation. By knowing the precise workings of karmic bondage, a practitioner can more effectively cultivate the three jewels and adopt practices that lead to the cessation of karmic inflow and the shedding of existing karmas.

In summary, “karma in Gommatasara” refers to a comprehensive, highly structured doctrine that explains the material nature of karma, its intricate classifications, its role in shaping spiritual stages, and the methods by which it can be overcome. Nemichandra’s Karma-kanda stands as a technical yet deeply spiritual guide, bridging metaphysical analysis with the lived path of purification and liberation.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara, Karma-kanda, Chapter 1 (Description of the Prakriti or Nature of Karmas)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
पणमिय सिरसा रोमिं गुणरय विभूसणं महावीरण् । सम्मत्तरणयनिलयं पयादसमुत्तिणं वोच्छं ॥ १ ॥
प्रकृतिः शीलं स्वभावः जीवाङ्गयोरणादिसम्बन्धः । कनकोपले मलम् वा तयोरस्तित्वं स्वयंसिद्धम् ॥ २ ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
paṇamiya sirasā romiṃ guṇaraya vibhūsaṇaṃ mahāvīraṃ |
sammattarāyaṇanilayaṃ payādasamuttiṇaṃ vocchaṃ || 1 ||
prakṛtiḥ śīlaṃ svabhāvaḥ jivāṅgayoraṇādisambandhaḥ |
kanakopale malam vā tayorastitvaṃ svayaṃ siddham || 2 ||
primary_sources.translation:
1. Having bowed with the head to Lord Nemi, adorned with the jewels of the pure soul’s attributes, a great hero and a mine of the gem of right-belief, I shall speak of the description of the Prakriti or nature of Karmas.
2. The eternal bondage of soul and karmic matter is their nature—prakriti, shila, svabhava. The existence of soul and karmas is self-proved, as is the dirt in golden ore.
primary_sources.notes: These opening verses of the Karma-kanda set the doctrinal frame for the discussion of karma. Nemichandra invokes Lord Nemi and then defines the union of soul and karmic matter as anadi-sambandha (beginningless connection), describing it as the soul’s nature (prakriti, shila, svabhava). The analogy of dirt in golden ore emphasizes that karmic impurity is real and coexistent with the soul, yet separable through purification. The passage is foundational for understanding Gommatasara’s assertion that karmic bondage is both ontologically real and soteriologically removable.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara, Karma-kanda, Classification and Ordering of Karmas
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text:
घातिव वेयणीयं मोहस्स बलेण घाददे जीवं । इदि घादीणं मज्झे मोहस्सादिम्हि पढिदं तु ॥ १६ ॥
घातिवत् वेदनीयं मोहस्य बलेन घातयति जीवम् । इति घातीनां मध्ये मोहस्यादौ पठितं तु ॥ १६ ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ghārdiva veyaṇīyaṃ mohassa baleṇa ghādade jīvaṃ |
idi ghādīṇaṃ majjhe mohassādimhi paḍhidaṃ tu || 16 ||
ghātivat vedanīyaṃ mohasyā balena ghātayati jīvam |
iti ghātīnāṃ madhye mohasyādau paṭhitaṃ tu || 16 ||
primary_sources.translation: 16. The Feeling (vedaniya) karma, by the force of the Deluding (mohaniya) karma, destroys, like the destructive karmas, the (real character of) the soul. Therefore it is placed in the middle of the destructive karmas and before the deluding karma.
primary_sources.notes: This verse explains why vedaniya (feeling-producing) karma is classified among the ghatiya (destructive) karmas and clarifies its position in the canonical list. Nemichandra notes that vedaniya operates with the support of deluding karma, producing occasions of pleasure and pain that can disturb the soul’s thought-activity when accompanied by indulgence (rati) and ennui (arati). The commentary further distinguishes destructive from non-destructive karmas and shows how the ordering of karmas reflects their functional relationships. This is a key passage for understanding the internal logic of the eightfold karmic classification in Gommatasara.

primary_sources.title: Gommatasara, Karma-kanda, Verse on Age and Status Karmas
primary_sources.author: Acharya Nemichandra Siddhanta Chakravarti
primary_sources.original_text: आयुर्बलेन अवस्थितिः भवस्य इति नाम आयुः पूर्व तु । भवमाश्रित्य नीचोच्चमिति गोत्रं नामपूर्वं तु ॥ १८ ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
āyurbalena avasthitiḥ bhavasya iti nāma āyuḥ pūrva tu |
bhavamāśritya nīcoccamiti gotraṃ nāmapūrvaṃ tu || 18 ||
primary_sources.translation: 18. By the power of the age (āyuḥ) karma, the sojourn of the souls in mundane existence is secured; therefore the age karma is mentioned before the body-making karma. High and low family (gotra) depends on the condition of existence; therefore the body-making karma is mentioned before the family-determining karma.
primary_sources.notes: Here Nemichandra explains the doctrinal rationale for the sequence of non-destructive karmas: age (āyushya), body-making (nāma), and status (gotra). Age karma determines the duration of a particular embodiment in samsara, so it is listed before body-making karma, which shapes the specific physical and psychophysical constitution. Status karma, determining high or low family and social standing, is dependent on the condition of existence established by the preceding karmas. This verse illustrates how Gommatasara links karmic taxonomy to the concrete conditions of worldly life, while still treating these karmas as ultimately removable impediments to liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Karma in Gommatasara is purely symbolic or psychological, not a real substance.
misconceptions.reality: Gommatasara consistently treats karma as a subtle form of pudgala (matter) that actually binds to the soul. Nemichandra uses analogies such as dirt in golden ore to emphasize that karmic impurity is materially real, even though it is extremely subtle. While karmic experiences have psychological dimensions, the text’s ontology is explicitly realist: karma is a dravya (substance) with specific modes and subtypes that can be classified, measured, and ultimately destroyed.

misconceptions.myth: All karmas in Gommatasara affect the soul in the same way and are equally harmful.
misconceptions.reality: Gommatasara carefully distinguishes between ghatiya (destructive) and aghatiya (non-destructive) karmas. The first four—knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, and deluding—directly impair the essential qualities of the soul, while the remaining four—obstructive, age, body-making, and status—affect external conditions of existence. Moreover, each karma has different subtypes, intensities, durations, and quantities, leading to a nuanced spectrum of effects rather than a uniform impact.

misconceptions.myth: Karmic bondage in Gommatasara is eternal and cannot be fully removed.
misconceptions.reality: Although Nemichandra describes the soul’s connection with karmic matter as beginningless (anadi), he is clear that it is not endless. The Karma-kanda explains in detail how right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, along with practices such as vows, austerities, and meditation, lead to samvara (stoppage of inflow) and nirjara (shedding) of karmas. The doctrine of the fourteen gunasthanas culminates in stages where all karmas are destroyed, resulting in moksha, the state of complete liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Gommatasara’s karma doctrine is only relevant for monks and has no application to lay life.
misconceptions.reality: While Gommatasara is highly technical and often used in advanced scholastic contexts, its karmic framework underlies Jain ethics for both monastics and laypeople. The text’s analysis of how passions and activities generate karmic bondage informs the rationale for lay vows, ethical disciplines, and gradual spiritual progress. Understanding karma in Gommatasara helps lay practitioners see how everyday actions contribute to or reduce karmic load, even if they do not engage with the full technical detail of the 148 sub-classes.
